We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with $1/f$ fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit $T_{1}$ decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the $l$-photon JCM ($l=1,2,3,4$), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.

AI.tldr: A two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model in a superconducting flux-qubit circuit is analyzed numerically to generate Schrödinger cat states, quantifying fidelity degradation from flux noise, qubit relaxation, and photon loss, and examining phase-state-basis dynamics and initial-temperature effects.
AI.motivation: Realizing macroscopic quantum superpositions in scalable solid-state platforms requires understanding which decoherence channels actually limit cat-state preparation, and how initially impure bosonic states affect the outcome.
AI.method: A specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation of the two-photon JCM is considered and the two-photon coupling constant estimated; numerical simulations of three noise sources (1/f magnetic flux noise, flux-qubit T1 relaxation, photon loss in the mode obtained by quantizing the dc-SQUID phase used for readout) are performed. The time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis is studied for l-photon JCM (l = 1,2,3,4) from a coherent state, and the unitary evolution from a displaced thermal state after decoupling from the bath is examined.
AI.result: Photon loss is found to be the dominant limitation on cat-state fidelity, more severe than flux noise or qubit relaxation. The Pegg-Barnett phase-basis dynamics reveal how the phase-amplitude distribution evolves for l = 1-4. Starting from a displaced thermal state, the initial temperature measurably degrades the fidelity and distorts the Wigner function of the generated cat states.
AI.conclusion: A superconducting-circuit two-photon JCM is a viable but loss-limited route to Schrödinger cat states; suppressing photon loss and minimizing initial thermal population are the key requirements for high-fidelity cat-state generation.

title: Curvature-Calibrated Friction and an Exact Gauge Symmetry for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027), IEEE Symposium for Multidisciplinary Computational Intelligence Incubators (IEEE MCII). Code: https://github.com/khoshisashi/qhd-curvature-friction
summary: A design problem constrained by a partial differential equation can be solved coherently on a quantum computer. The objective is block-encoded rather than measured, and Quantum Hamiltonian Descent consumes it directly. We identify two obstacles in this pipeline and repair both. First, the oracle construction assumes affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, which covariance entries violate for every off-diagonal generator. Encoding the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms restores both conditions at every register point, at the price of a representational floor, median 45% of the fitted family's own objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary and 22% with a variable diagonal. Second, adding a constant to the objective leaves the measurement distribution exactly invariant, yet the mean-objective friction heuristic in current use assigns such objectives different schedules. Calibrating the friction to the landscape curvature restores the symmetry, though not the constant in $ν= c\sqrtμ$, and a bracketed sweep at matched objective-phase exposure, not end-to-end cost, places the best tested friction between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping on a diffusion-design benchmark, a broad plateau an order of magnitude below the classical default.

AI.tldr: PDE-constrained design problems can be tackled coherently on a quantum computer using block-encoded objectives driven by Quantum Hamiltonian Descent; two obstacles (oracle construction and friction-schedule calibration) are identified and repaired.
AI.motivation: Standard oracle constructions for QHD assume affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, and the mean-objective friction heuristic breaks the invariance of the measurement distribution under adding a constant to the objective—both hinder a coherent, measurement-free design pipeline for PDE-constrained problems.
AI.method: Encode the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms so both oracle conditions hold at every register point; calibrate the friction heuristic to landscape curvature to restore constant-shift symmetry; evaluate a bracketed sweep at matched objective-phase exposure on a diffusion-design benchmark.
AI.result: The atom decomposition incurs a representational floor (median 45% of the fitted family's objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary, 22% with a variable diagonal). Curvature calibration restores the constant-shift symmetry but not the additive constant in ν = c√μ. The best tested friction lies between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping, a broad plateau an order of magnitude below the classical default.
AI.conclusion: Both pipeline obstacles are repairable, yielding a coherent quantum design loop, but the fixes carry a quantifiable representational floor and calibrate friction only up to an unresolved additive constant, with optimal friction well below the classical default.

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
summary: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

AI.tldr: A basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization that casts the RVE reduced energy as a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian, enabling homogenized stress to be extracted directly from the same computational-basis measurements as the energy.
AI.motivation: Computational homogenization requires repeated RVE solves to obtain effective response and homogenized stress, which is costly; a quantum formulation could offer an alternative route while avoiding extra measurement overhead for stress recovery.
AI.method: The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a QUBO problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Stress observables are derived via the Hellmann–Feynman theorem by differentiating the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to prescribed macroscopic strain. Ground states are approximated with VQE and the scheme is demonstrated on a 2D periodic RVE.
AI.result: Although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local: strain-independent two-qubit couplings vanish under differentiation, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-Z terms. These are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian, so homogenized stress is recovered from the same measurements without reconstructing the microscopic displacement field or using an additional basis.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields homogenized stress directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational-basis measurements as the energy, and is demonstrated on a 2D periodic RVE, offering a measurement-efficient route to quantum computational homogenization.

title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
summary: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.

AI.tldr: Error-correction failure attribution is pairing-dependent under non-Pauli noise; cause sets differ starkly from Pauli-twirl predictions despite equivalent failure rates.
AI.motivation: Under Pauli noise, attributing a stabilizer-memory failure to its causative noise has a canonical answer, but under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with counterfactuals—an ambiguity the paper aims to expose and resolve.
AI.method: Defines a failing shot's "cause set" (sites whose removal alone removes the failure) and distinguishes it from pairing-independent net effects. Analyzes where pairing enters—at every step a fixed random draw meets a Born probability—showing maximal coupling selects shared random numbers while continuity does not. Compares exact non-Pauli noise against its Pauli twirl in a distance-three surface code.
AI.result: Exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites versus 2.3% under the twirl. Admissible pairings move mean coherent cause count from 1.61 up to 80 times the marginal-allowed minimum, while pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models.
AI.conclusion: Shot-level attributions are not canonical under non-Pauli noise and must state their pairing. Practitioners should report pairing-independent effects alongside shot-level attributions, since equivalent failure rates mask divergent causal structure.

title: Interfacing Silicon Nitride Nanophotonics with Cuprous Oxide Rydberg Excitons
summary: Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O), the solid-state counterpart of Rydberg atoms, are hydrogen-like electron--hole quasi-particles with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions that promise optical nonlinearities at the few-photon level. Exploiting them in a waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) setting can enable what atomic Rydberg platforms achieve only with ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling/trapping---a guided optical mode interfaced with the Rydberg medium---while adding the scalability and advanced fabrication of integrated photonics. Here we demonstrate a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface of Cu$_2$O Rydberg excitons with a SiN$_x$ nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission from the Cu$_2$O microcrystal is coupled to the guided mode, routed along the waveguide, and collected from an output grating. The spectrum shows the phonon-assisted 1$s$ orthoexciton emission together with the low-lying 2$p$ and 3$p$ lines of the yellow Rydberg series. Spatially selective excitation excludes substrate background and direct scatter, and the enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal identifies the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel. These results establish the complete material--device--measurement stack for a novel platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics based on Rydberg excitons.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates a CMOS-compatible SiNx nanophotonic waveguide interfaced with Cu2O Rydberg excitons, collecting guided excitonic emission including 2p and 3p Rydberg lines.
AI.motivation: Rydberg excitons in Cu2O offer Rydberg-atom-like strong interactions and micron-scale wavefunctions without vacuum/laser-cooling overhead; integrating them into waveguide QED promises few-photon optical nonlinearities with photonic integration scalability.
AI.method: A monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface coupling a Cu2O microcrystal to a SiNx nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission is coupled to the guided mode, routed, and out-coupled via a grating. Spatially selective excitation suppresses substrate background and direct scatter; polarization analysis identifies the TE-like guided mode.
AI.result: The collected spectrum shows phonon-assisted 1s orthoexciton emission together with low-lying 2p and 3p lines of the yellow Rydberg series. Enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal confirms the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel; spatial selectivity excludes parasitic background.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a complete material-device-measurement stack for a Rydberg-exciton-based platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics.

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
summary: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

AI.tldr: The paper derives one-shot bounds on the number of independent quantum systems needed to hide a correlated system, expressed via binary hypothesis tests and hypothesis-testing relative entropy, and applies them to private communication and secret-key distillation.
AI.motivation: Determining how many independent (decoupled-from-reference) systems suffice to "hide" one system correlated with a reference is central to decoupling and convex-split arguments, but sharp one-shot control over the required number of systems—valid for general density operators on separable Hilbert spaces—was lacking.
AI.method: Any joint measurement on the hidden system, the independent systems, and the reference is converted into binary tests on a single system plus the reference. For each test, the probability of a false signal (independent pair prepared) is bounded. Averaging the largest signal-acceptance probabilities permitted by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma; a second bound yields a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the reference state. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions over the hidden system's location gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret-key distillation, accounting for public eavesdropper information.
AI.result: For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private/key bits from n independent repetitions are recovered, and the residual loss is bounded by log2 n + O(1) at fixed error. A position-based key-distillation protocol attains this bound using O(n) public bits.
AI.conclusion: Binary hypothesis testing provides a tight, one-shot operational handle on the number of independent systems required for hiding correlated systems; the resulting bounds unify one-shot private communication and secret-key distillation and are asymptotically tight up to log2 n + O(1) with efficient O(n) public communication.

title: Remote Use of Quantum Machines in the Adversarial Scenario
summary: Networked quantum technologies allow users to operate quantum machines hosted by remote servers, but classical commands alone cannot ensure that only the intended user can prepare the useful inputs that activate them. We formulate the problem of adversarial remote use of quantum machines in the framework of quantum resource theories. A device controlled by Bob is correlated to a remote user, Alice, through a bipartite state, and also to an adversary Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's machine by remotely preparing its inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Remote use is truly advantageous when Alice is guaranteed to unlock a larger average task value than the adversary Eve, given the same marginal state of Bob. We show that for tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, where the figure of merit is invariant under unitary operations, by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity one machine but not another. Finally, we order Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder, based on the ensembles each party can prepare on Bob's side. Shared quantum correlations thereby become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes adversarial remote use of networked quantum machines in a resource-theoretic framework, showing that exclusivity of access is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, an entanglement imbalance.
AI.motivation: Networked quantum technologies let users operate remote quantum machines, but classical authentication cannot guarantee that only the intended user can prepare the input states needed to activate the machine. A framework is needed to characterize when a legitimate remote user (Alice) has a genuine advantage over an adversary (Eve).
AI.method: A device controlled by Bob is correlated with Alice through a bipartite state, with Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete by remotely preparing inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. The authors formalize the problem within quantum resource theories, requiring that Alice unlock a larger average task value than Eve given Bob's same marginal state. They analyze convex figures of merit via complementary upper roofs, spectral (unitary-invariant) tasks via an entanglement imbalance, and order the parties' full programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder based on preparable ensembles.
AI.result: For tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs; for spectral tasks it is governed by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Applications to purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity for one machine but not another.
AI.conclusion: Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers are ordered by a task-independent simulation preorder grounded in the ensembles each can prepare on Bob's side, establishing shared quantum correlations as a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.

title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
summary:
We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.
  We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.

AI.tldr: This paper maps the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states (fixed points) of bounded-degree polynomial bosonic Lindbladians, spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability.
AI.motivation: Transient bosonic dynamics complexity is known, but the computational power of bosonic fixed points is unexplored and requires handling infinite-dimensional subtleties: existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.
AI.method: Analyze bounded-degree polynomial Lindbladian dynamics: embed quantum circuits into fixed-point observable estimation; characterize Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping and Kerr perturbations classically; and reduce boson-sampling and RE-hard problems to stationary-state tasks.
AI.result: Universal quantum computation embeds into fixed-point observable estimation with degree-12 Hamiltonian and linear loss, preparable from vacuum in polynomial time; Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping admit efficient photon-number sampling, stable under weak Kerr perturbations; Gaussian fixed points without pumping are hard to sample exactly (constant loss) and approximately (inverse-polynomial loss) under boson-sampling conjectures; non-Gaussian fixed-point sampling relates to boson-sampling variants; deciding stationary-state existence is RE-hard even for degree-5 jump operators on ≤4 modes.
AI.conclusion: Bosonic fixed points exhibit a rich complexity landscape from universal quantum computation to undecidability, establishing both quantum power and hardness results.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
summary: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified framework for sensing time-dependent (AC) fields via classical pulse-sequence protocols and quantum algorithms, achieving optimal sensitivity and a beyond-Heisenberg limit that requires quantum computation and persists under noise.
AI.motivation: Conventional AC sensing (e.g., dynamical decoupling) is suboptimal and limited by the standard quantum limit, and it is unclear what fundamental sensitivity quantum mechanics permits and whether quantum computation can exceed classical sensing strategies, especially under noise.
AI.method: Three new pulse-sequence protocols—randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy—are developed for optimal linear/nonlinear AC sensing on spin/qubit platforms. Then quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS) couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor via two primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb converting any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and quantum algorithms extracting signal information in superposition, implementable with one memory ancilla.
AI.result: The protocols attain optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing, improving existing devices by changing only pulse sequences. QCS reaches the ultimate quantum-mechanical limit, which lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit. Under constant-strength sensor depolarization with noise aligned to the signal, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling while any non-quantum-computational protocol is proven limited to standard-quantum-limit scaling—the first asymptotic beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and positions quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with advantages surpassing the Heisenberg limit that persist under noise and showing Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing.

title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
summary: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

AI.tldr: GEARS is a runtime calibration framework for quantum error correction that amplifies gate errors to strengthen syndrome-based calibration signals, cutting measurement needs ~8x and reducing logical failures 31-40% in surface-code simulations.
AI.motivation: Hours-long quantum computations require repeated calibration to counter hardware drift. Conventional calibration removes qubits from the code, incurring space-time overhead. Syndrome-based in-situ calibration avoids this but faces a trade-off: more measurements slow control updates, while stronger probe perturbations create larger signals but introduce extra errors.
AI.method: GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with gate-error amplification. It repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing.
AI.result: Surface code simulations show depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements ~8x at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration it reduces excess expected logical failures by ~31-40% versus calibration without amplification, and under time-dependent drift it raises the estimated critical drift frequency by ~1.9x.
AI.conclusion: Deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

title: Insurance portfolio simulation with a quantum circuit
summary: A central challenge in actuarial science is characterising the distribution of losses generated by an insurance portfolio. Copulas provide a natural framework for modelling joint distributions, but flexible high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling remains challenging in practice. We propose a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) approach adapted to insurance portfolios, combining (i) a tail-focused discretisation of heavy-tailed marginals, (ii) a Monte Carlo-style objective function that enables the numerical precision of the algorithm to scale when trained on a relatively small number of samples, and (iii) a two-stage hierarchical training scheme enabling efficient training on a simulator and fine-tuning on quantum hardware. On a mixed portfolio of equity returns and insurance losses, the trained circuit recovers the qualitative dependence structure, with near-independence between equity and losses and positive dependence among loss lines. Exponential quantile encoding substantially improves the fit to the tail of the aggregate loss distribution relative to a uniform encoding, and the hierarchical scheme substantially outperforms single-stage training of a circuit of the same size from random initialisation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Quantum Circuit Born Machine adapted to insurance portfolios for flexible high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling, combining tail-focused discretisation, a Monte Carlo objective, and hierarchical training.
AI.motivation: Characterising the loss distribution of an insurance portfolio is a central actuarial challenge. Copulas model joint distributions naturally, but flexible high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling remain difficult in practice.
AI.method: A QCBM adapted to insurance portfolios with (i) a tail-focused discretisation of heavy-tailed marginals, (ii) a Monte Carlo-style objective letting numerical precision scale when trained on relatively few samples, and (iii) a two-stage hierarchical training scheme for efficient simulator training and hardware fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a mixed portfolio of equity returns and insurance losses, the trained circuit recovers the qualitative dependence structure—near-independence between equity and losses, positive dependence among loss lines. Exponential quantile encoding substantially improves tail fit of aggregate losses versus uniform encoding, and the hierarchical scheme substantially outperforms single-stage training from random initialisation at equal circuit size.
AI.conclusion: The QCBM approach offers a practical route to high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling for insurance portfolios, with tail-focused encoding and hierarchical training providing clear empirical advantages.

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transversal controlled-Z gate across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture, using a tailored dynamical decoupling scheme with a genuine geometric cancellation to enable simultaneous pairwise entangling operations with fewer pulses, and assesses decoherence, crosstalk from laser wave-vector misalignment, and fault-tolerant impact on a logical Bell state.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs high-fidelity entangling gates that can be applied efficiently across many qubit pairs simultaneously; sequential two-qubit gates are slow and resource-intensive, motivating parallel (transversal) entangling operations.
AI.method: A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings among neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion register, with pulse count scaling quadratically in ion number; a genuine geometric cancellation is incorporated to reduce pulse count and, for selected register sizes, complete the parallel operation faster than an equivalent two-qubit-gate sequence while needing a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. Experimental feasibility is analyzed via decoherence and crosstalk from laser wave-vector misalignment, and crosstalk-induced gate errors are studied in fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two [[4,1,2]] quantum-error-detection code blocks.
AI.result: The geometric cancellation reduces pulse count and, for selected register sizes, outperforms the equivalent sequential two-qubit-gate sequence in speed while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency; decoherence and crosstalk (wave-vector misalignment) effects are quantified, and crosstalk-induced gate errors are shown to influence fault-tolerant logical Bell-state preparation between two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
AI.conclusion: Transversal entangling gates in double-well trapped-ion architectures are a promising building block for scalable, trapped-ion-based fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

AI.tldr: In supervised quantum classification, exploiting label information via boosting of noisy parameterized circuits achieves the same margin-based risk bound as PEC but needs fewer circuit executions as depth and noise grow, avoiding the cost of noiseless-output reconstruction.
AI.motivation: QEM generally incurs superpolynomial/exponential sampling overhead when recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information. The authors ask whether problem-specific information—here, labeled examples in supervised quantum machine learning—can reduce the sampling needed. Binary classification is a natural testbed because correct prediction depends only on the sign and margin of the classifier output, not on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value.
AI.method: The authors build a theoretical and empirical framework comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits against probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), constrained to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, they establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound showing that matching empirical margin loss yields the same upper bound on expected classification risk. They then derive resource criteria and run finite-shot teacher-student simulations evaluating AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost across circuit depth and physical noise strength.
AI.result: Under identical classification-accuracy targets, boosting requires fewer circuit executions than PEC, with the advantage growing with circuit depth and noise strength. Boosting also attains higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference method.
AI.conclusion: For the supervised-learning problems studied, the results show a task-dependent resource advantage: using information retained in noisy outputs can bypass the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

title: Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Differential Privacy
summary:
Differential privacy has been successfully extended to quantum computing and information processing, where sensitive data are encoded in quantum states and protected by quantum noise mechanisms that keep the outcomes of any measurement on neighboring states nearly indistinguishable. In the quantum setting, however, the state submitted to a quantum computer may be entangled with a hidden reference system secretly held by an adversary. Such entanglement cannot be detected from the submitted state alone, and it poses a challenge with no counterpart in the classical setting. Existing frameworks of quantum differential privacy consider only measurements on the released state, leaving this scenario largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we identify the entanglement attack: an adversary submits one half of an entangled state to a quantum computer that runs a privacy mechanism, keeps the other half, and finally measures both halves jointly. We show that this attack may completely break a mechanism that satisfies quantum differential privacy with a finite parameter, driving its privacy parameter to infinity. To counter it, we propose entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), a privacy framework that is native to quantum entanglement and remains valid against such attacks. We characterize exactly when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter $\varepsilon^*_{\mathrm{EA}}$ of any quantum mechanism can be computed by a semidefinite programming problem (SDP). Building on this, we quantify the extra privacy leakage caused by entanglement and show that it can be bounded by choosing appropriate mechanisms, with the depolarizing channel being our recommended choice. Finally, we demonstrate both the attack and its countermeasure on simulated and physical quantum hardware, and the experimental results agree with our theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an entanglement attack that breaks existing quantum differential privacy (QDP) by exploiting entanglement with an adversary-held reference system, and proposes entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP) to defend against it.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum differential privacy frameworks only consider measurements on the released state, ignoring that a submitted state may be entangled with a hidden reference system held by an adversary. This entanglement cannot be detected from the submitted state alone and has no classical counterpart, leaving a critical gap in the privacy analysis.
AI.method: The authors formalize the entanglement attack, where an adversary submits half of an entangled state, keeps the other half, and jointly measures both halves. They then introduce entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), characterize when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter epsilon*_EA can be computed via a semidefinite programming (SDP) problem. They also analyze and bound the extra privacy leakage caused by entanglement.
AI.result: The entanglement attack can completely break a mechanism satisfying QDP with a finite parameter, driving its privacy parameter to infinity. EA-QDP remains valid against such attacks, and its optimal parameter is computable via SDP. The extra privacy leakage from entanglement can be bounded by choosing appropriate mechanisms, with the depolarizing channel recommended. Experiments on simulated and physical quantum hardware confirm the theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement poses a fundamental threat to conventional quantum differential privacy, and EA-QDP provides a principled framework that stays robust under entanglement attacks, with practical guidance for mechanism design and experimental validation.

title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
summary: Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.

AI.tldr: Gate ordering that changes fault propagation is optimized via CP-SAT synthesis that shares relative gate orders across grouped checks of structured CSS codes, yielding lower logical error rates and much faster feasible-circuit discovery than ASC, PropHunt and AlphaSyndrome.
AI.motivation: Gate orders can alter fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits realize the same ideal stabilizer measurements, but optimizing orders independently for every check becomes computationally prohibitive as code size grows. This motivates a scalable synthesis approach that reduces the number of independent ordering choices.
AI.method: A synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit; noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide selection of the final circuit.
AI.result: Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, the method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates; versus ASC (strongest baseline), the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest 38.6%. Circuit-level distance improves over ASC on ten instances and is preserved in seven. Across five timed codes, mean time to the first feasible circuit is reduced by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC at equal or lower depth.
AI.conclusion: Sharing relative gate orders across connectivity groups makes gate-order optimization tractable and effective, delivering lower logical error rates, competitive-or-better circuit-level distance, and dramatically faster synthesis than state-of-the-art methods.

title: Nonmagnetic Impurity Effects on Majorana Braiding Quantum Gates in Vortex Cores
summary: Using time-dependent many-body simulations, we investigate nonmagnetic impurity effects on vortex-core Majorana braiding. In the two-MZM $\sqrt{Z}$ gate, sufficiently strong attractive impurities suppress the topological gap $Δ_t$, reduce adiabaticity, and degrade the quantization of the geometric-phase difference; the repulsive impurities considered here cause no comparable damage despite stronger zero-energy nonequilibrium local density of states (LDOS) distortions. Slowing the braid or using a $2a_0$ detour restores near-quantization in the cases examined. In the four-MZM configuration, attractive impurities leave the low-energy spectrum nearly unchanged, whereas repulsive impurities mainly suppress the first excited state. Slower braiding substantially improves the $X$ gate success probability. A specific attractive-impurity pair yields near-unit success ($\approx 0.9985$), unlike two weak repulsive impurities. These findings clarify how nonmagnetic impurities affect the low-energy spectrum and adiabatic dynamics of vortex-core Majorana braiding and provide theoretical guidance for designing robust braiding protocols in realistic topological superconducting platforms.

AI.tldr: Time-dependent many-body simulations show that nonmagnetic impurities can differentially degrade vortex-core Majorana braiding: attractive impurities hurt the two-MZM √Z gate by suppressing the topological gap and adiabaticity, while repulsive impurities mainly affect the four-MZM X gate via excited-state suppression; slowing the braid or using a detour restores near-quantization in tested cases.
AI.motivation: Realistic topological superconducting platforms contain nonmagnetic impurities whose influence on the low-energy spectrum and adiabatic dynamics of vortex-core Majorana braiding is not well understood, motivating a systematic study of how such disorder affects braiding fidelity and gate quantization.
AI.method: Time-dependent many-body simulations of vortex-core Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in two configurations: a two-MZM √Z geometric-phase gate and a four-MZM X gate, with attractive and repulsive nonmagnetic impurities introduced and braiding speed and path (including a 2a₀ detour) varied.
AI.result: In the two-MZM √Z gate, sufficiently strong attractive impurities suppress the topological gap Δ_t, reduce adiabaticity, and degrade geometric-phase-difference quantization; repulsive impurities cause no comparable damage despite stronger zero-energy nonequilibrium LDOS distortions. Slowing the braid or a 2a₀ detour restores near-quantization. In the four-MZM case, attractive impurities leave the low-energy spectrum nearly unchanged while repulsive impurities mainly suppress the first excited state; slower braiding substantially improves X-gate success probability, and a specific attractive-impurity pair yields ≈0.9985 success versus failure with two weak repulsive impurities.
AI.conclusion: Nonmagnetic impurities affect vortex-core Majorana braiding in a configuration- and impurity-type-dependent manner, clarifying disorder effects on the low-energy spectrum and adiabatic dynamics and offering theoretical guidance for robust braiding protocols in realistic topological superconducting platforms.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
comment: 5 main pages, 2 main figures. 15 total pages. Accepted in NeurIPS 2026 EvoRobust Workshop
summary: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: A domain-specific language (DSL) capturing published belief-propagation decoders for quantum LDPC codes enables both manual re-parameterisation and grammatical-evolution search, yielding decoders 17–41× faster (BP+OSD-0 ~103× faster than the tuned ldpc package) and new evolved decoders on the time-error front.
AI.motivation: Quantum decoding requires fast, reliable noise correction. Existing BP-based decoders for qLDPC codes are hand-tuned and slow; the authors want an intermediate representation that exposes expert knowledge explicitly so it can be improved both manually and automatically, bridging human intuition and machine-driven optimization.
AI.method: Several published BP decoders are expressed in a Domain-Specific Language. The explicit parameterisation allows re-parameterising BP+OSD and BP+LSD decoders with damping prior to search. A grammatical evolution search over the DSL is then used to discover new decoder variants, evaluated on metrics of logical error rate versus decoding time.
AI.result: Re-parameterised BP+OSD and BP+LSD decoders are 17.1–41.0× faster at higher error rate; BP+OSD-0 is ~103× faster than ldpc's tuned version on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. An evolved decoder makes 23% fewer logical errors than damped BP+OSD-0 at 0.64× its time; decoders evolved from random code outperform ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at ≤1/31 of its time. The two fastest evolved decoders, frozen at one operating point, generalize across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying on the time-error front.
AI.conclusion: Embedding expert knowledge in a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization, unlocking highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: High-fidelity control of long-lived data qubits via a noisy mediator
summary: Long-lived qubits are attractive for storing quantum information, but they are often difficult to control or couple directly. A common strategy is to use mediator qubits to generate effective interactions for gate implementation. However, the mediator typically has a shorter coherence time than the data qubits, so mediator relaxation and dephasing are expected to limit the achievable gate fidelity. Here, we show that this limitation can be overcome. We present a reset-assisted control method that suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on a quantum register of long-lived data qubits. Although mediator quantum jumps render the data-qubit evolution stochastic, repeated mediator reinitialization drives the resulting evolution paths toward the desired target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis reveals the physical mechanism of error suppression and provides compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms. Our results relax the requirement for long mediator coherence, broadening the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity control.

AI.tldr: A reset-assisted control method suppresses mediator-induced errors, enabling high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on long-lived data qubits despite short mediator coherence, with analytical quantum-trajectory analysis explaining the error suppression mechanism.
AI.motivation: Long-lived qubits are ideal for storing quantum information but are hard to control or couple directly. Mediator qubits are used to generate effective interactions, yet mediators typically have shorter coherence times than data qubits, so mediator relaxation and dephasing are expected to limit achievable gate fidelity.
AI.method: The authors introduce a reset-assisted control scheme in which repeated reinitialization (reset) of the mediator qubit is applied, so that although mediator quantum jumps make the data-qubit evolution stochastic, the repeated reinitialization drives the resulting evolution paths toward the desired target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis is used to derive the underlying error-suppression mechanism and compact fidelity formulas that allow the method to be adapted across platforms.
AI.result: The reset-assisted method suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on a register of long-lived data qubits, overcoming the fidelity limitation normally imposed by mediator relaxation and dephasing.
AI.conclusion: Mediator coherence is not a hard requirement for high-fidelity control: the results relax the need for long mediator coherence and broaden the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity quantum gates.

title: A New Quantum Algorithm Framework for Integer Order Entropy Estimation
summary: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a basic problem in statistical property estimation. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm framework for estimating Rényi entropy with fixed integer order $k\geq 2$. Given purified quantum query-access to a distribution on $n$ symbols, our algorithm estimates its order-$k$ Rényi entropy to within additive error $ε$ using $$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{n^{u_k}}{ε^{1-u_k}} + \frac{n^{(k-1)/(2k)}}ε\right)$$ queries, where $u_k=\max_{2\leq j\leq k} \frac{(3k-j)2^{j-2}-k}{k(2^j-1)}$. The main ingredient is a recursive construction of collision states in which intermediate states are retained and reused. We bound both the preparation and reflection costs, and choose the number of retained states at each order so that all recursive steps fit within a common query budget. We combine this construction with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, estimating the contribution of the labels found along the way separately from the remaining power sum. A batch estimator gives the required bound in the high-precision regime, and an initial search removes the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum algorithm framework that estimates Rényi entropy of fixed integer order k≥2 for an unknown distribution over n symbols, achieving additive error ε with query complexity Õ(n^{u_k}/ε^{1−u_k} + n^{(k−1)/(2k)}ε), where u_k is an explicit function of k, via recursively constructed and reused collision states combined with threshold-based power-sum estimation.
AI.motivation: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a fundamental problem in statistical property estimation. Estimating Rényi entropy (order k≥2) quantumly with query access is the target, extending classical statistical estimation to the quantum query model.
AI.method: A recursive construction of collision states where intermediate states are retained and reused. The authors bound both preparation and reflection costs and select the number of retained states at each order so all recursive steps fit within a common query budget. This is combined with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, estimating contributions of labels found along the way separately from the remaining power sum. A batch estimator handles the high-precision regime, and an initial search removes the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.
AI.result: Improved query complexity Õ(n^{u_k}/ε^{1−u_k} + n^{(k−1)/(2k)}ε) with u_k = max_{2≤j≤k} ((3k−j)2^{j−2} − k)/(k(2^j−1)), for estimating order-k Rényi entropy to additive error ε given purified quantum query access.
AI.conclusion: A quantum framework achieves efficient Rényi entropy estimation for fixed integer order k≥2 through recursive collision-state construction with reuse, threshold decomposition, a batch estimator, and an initial search eliminating prior knowledge requirements.

title: Flat bands and bound states in the continuum in non-Hermitian pseudospin lattices
summary: Flat bands support compact localized states (CLSs), whereas bound states in the continuum (BICs) remain spatially localized despite having energies embedded in the continuum of extended states. Here, we investigate the connection between these phenomena in a class of one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices whose Bloch Hamiltonians take the pseudospin form H(k)=d(k)S. For integer pseudospin, the Hamiltonian intrinsically supports a zero-energy flat band and its associated compact localized states. When the effective pseudospin field has real transverse components and a purely imaginary longitudinal component, increasing non-Hermiticity compresses the dispersive bands toward the intrinsic zero-energy flat band, enabling their spectral overlap within a finite parameter range. The CLSs thus become embedded in the dispersive continuum and emerge as BICs. Adding a momentum-dependent Hermitian component along the gain-loss direction generally removes this spectral overlap without destroying the CLSs. We further extend this spectral mechanism to integer-pseudospin-n systems. These findings establish a connection between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation through non-Hermitian spectral reconstruction.

AI.tldr: In 1D non-Hermitian lattices with pseudospin Hamiltonians H(k)=d(k)·S, increasing non-Hermiticity compresses dispersive bands onto an intrinsic zero-energy flat band, embedding compact localized states in the continuum and turning them into bound states in the continuum (BICs).
AI.motivation: Flat bands host compact localized states (CLSs) and BICs are localized states embedded in a continuum, but the two phenomena are typically treated separately. The authors seek a unifying connection between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation.
AI.method: Study a class of one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices whose Bloch Hamiltonians take the pseudospin form H(k)=d(k)·S. For integer pseudospin the Hamiltonian intrinsically supports a zero-energy flat band with associated CLSs. The effective pseudospin field is given real transverse components and a purely imaginary longitudinal (gain-loss) component, and non-Hermiticity is tuned to drive spectral overlap; the mechanism is extended to integer-pseudospin-n systems, and a momentum-dependent Hermitian term along the gain-loss direction is added as a control.
AI.result: Increasing non-Hermiticity compresses the dispersive bands toward the intrinsic zero-energy flat band, producing spectral overlap within a finite parameter range; the CLSs then become embedded in the dispersive continuum and emerge as BICs. Adding a momentum-dependent Hermitian component along the gain-loss direction generally removes this spectral overlap while preserving the CLSs. The spectral mechanism generalizes to integer-pseudospin-n systems.
AI.conclusion: A connection between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation is established via non-Hermitian spectral reconstruction, offering a design principle for engineering BICs from flat-band CLSs.

title: The influence of quantum scarring on the onset of Bohmian chaos
summary: In the present work we investigate how the stable and unstable periodic orbits of a perturbed two-dimensional oscillator influence the Bohmian trajectories of the corresponding quantum system. In particular, we find that in our systems all Bohmian trajectories become chaotic in the long run and examine the times needed for them to approach their ergodic pattern. We show that these times are systematically shorter for orbits close to unstable periodic orbits than for orbits close to stable periodic orbits of the same period. We demonstrate that this behaviour is connected to scarring effects associated with both unstable and stable periodic orbits. We also investigate how the Bohmian dynamics changes when a stable periodic orbit undergoes a bifurcation and becomes unstable.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how stable and unstable periodic orbits of a perturbed 2D oscillator shape the Bohmian trajectories of the corresponding quantum system, finding all trajectories eventually become chaotic and that the times to reach ergodic behavior are shorter near unstable periodic orbits than near stable ones, linked to scarring effects.
AI.motivation: To understand how the classical orbit structure (stable vs. unstable periodic orbits) of a perturbed two-dimensional oscillator influences the quantum dynamics as described by Bohmian trajectories, including the ergodic approach and the role of scarring.
AI.method: Analysis of Bohmian (de Broglie–Bohm) trajectories in a quantum system whose classical counterpart is a perturbed two-dimensional oscillator, comparing trajectories initialized near stable and unstable periodic orbits of equal period; measurement of the times required to approach an ergodic pattern; examination of scarring effects; comparison of cases where a stable periodic orbit undergoes a bifurcation into an unstable one.
AI.result: All Bohmian trajectories become chaotic in the long run. The approach times to the ergodic pattern are systematically shorter for orbits close to unstable periodic orbits than for those close to stable periodic orbits of the same period. This behavior is connected to scarring effects associated with both unstable and stable periodic orbits, and it changes when a stable periodic orbit bifurcates into an unstable one.
AI.conclusion: The stability character of the underlying periodic orbits governs the rate at which Bohmian trajectories approach ergodicity, with unstable orbits yielding faster chaoticization; scarring is the mechanism linking classical orbit stability to quantum (Bohmian) dynamics, and bifurcations of periodic orbits modify the Bohmian dynamics accordingly.

title: Finite-Key Analysis for Multiple-Antenna Quantum Key Distribution with Continuous Variables
comment: The paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)
summary: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) techniques, known for their use in wireless communications, can also find applications in quantum communications systems. This is, for instance, relevant to satellite-based quantum communications when atmospheric turbulence and the time-varying nature of the channel can make their implementation difficult. Here, we study the application of MIMO techniques to continuous-variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) in the realistic setting where a finite number of signals are exchanged. We show how data collected during the brief overpass time of low-earth-orbit satellites over ground stations can be processed to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate. For $2\times 2$ MIMO settings with Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection, our finite-key analysis indicates that MIMO CV-QKD could outperform both multiplexed (with a nominal 3~dB improvement) and single-mode (with a nominal 6~dB nominal improvement) scenarios. Furthermore, we conjecture that the ultimate enhancement of a multiple-antenna CV-QKD system can be characterized by the product of the number of its inputs and outputs.

AI.tldr: MIMO techniques are applied to finite-key continuous-variable QKD for satellite links; a 2x2 MIMO setup with Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection yields key-rate gains of ~3 dB over multiplexed and ~6 dB over single-mode schemes.
AI.motivation: Satellite-based quantum communications suffer from atmospheric turbulence and time-varying channels, and MIMO techniques—proven in wireless communications—may mitigate these impairments in CV-QKD.
AI.method: Finite-key analysis of MIMO CV-QKD operating during the brief low-Earth-orbit overpass time; processing of collected data to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate, for 2x2 MIMO with Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection.
AI.result: MIMO CV-QKD outperforms multiplexed (nominal 3 dB) and single-mode (nominal 6 dB) scenarios in the finite-key regime.
AI.conclusion: MIMO offers a practical route to enhanced satellite CV-QKD, with the ultimate enhancement conjectured to scale as the product of the numbers of inputs and outputs.

title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
summary: Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "classical complexity" as the minimum classical-communication cost to simulate quantum preparations, proves it equals the classical communication needed to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, characterizes its scaling (exponential in quantum dimension, power-law in inverse noise), and provides certification tools including exact SDP, analytical witnesses, and scalable convex programs.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication naturally transmits quantum information, but it is unclear how difficult it is to achieve such transmission using only classical communication resources. The authors aim to quantify the fundamental cost of classically simulating quantum state transmission and to connect it to the simulation of quantum correlations.
AI.method: They introduce classical communication models for quantum preparations and define their minimum cost as classical complexity. They prove this complexity equals the classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. They then characterize the classical complexity of noisy quantum state space and develop certification tools: an exact semidefinite-programming characterization, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations, and convex programming scalable to hundreds or thousands of qubit states.
AI.result: The classical complexity equals the classical communication needed to simulate prepare-and-broadcast correlations, giving a resource equivalence. Its scaling grows exponentially with quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise, revealing rapidly scaling fundamental simulation cost. Certification is achieved via exact SDP characterization, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations, and convex programs scalable to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states.
AI.conclusion: Classical complexity is established as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory, and practical tools are provided for certifying it in quantum preparation devices.

title: Local-channel inequivalence within analytic symmetry-broken phases
summary: Gibbs states at different temperatures can be inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels even within a single phase with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry and analytic free energy. We prove this for the symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of a canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and a classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in $d\ge3$ dimensions. At lower temperatures, two distant observers can estimate the shared direction of order more accurately. The maximum mutual information they can obtain by separate measurements grows logarithmically with the radius of their regions. The leading term is the same throughout each ordered phase, while the constant term $\mathcal{C}(T)=\tfrac12\ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is strictly larger at lower temperatures. Here $Υ(T)$ is the phase stiffness and $c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ depends only on the region geometry. A quasi-local channel cannot increase this constant, so it is invariant under two-way conversion. Cooling would increase it and is therefore impossible between any two distinct temperatures in the ordered phase. On finite lattices, cooling with vanishing error requires a circuit whose causal radius grows at least linearly with the lattice side length. We also obtain the invariant for quantum and multicomponent Villain models and conjecture a stiffness formula for more general patterns of continuous symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: Gibbs states of an ideal Bose gas and the classical vortex-free Villain model at different temperatures in an ordered phase are inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels, because a mutual-information constant C(T)=½ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_geom increases monotonically as temperature decreases and is thus a quasi-local invariant.
AI.motivation: Standard lore ties distinct thermodynamic phases to distinct Gibbs-state equivalence classes, but it is unclear whether temperatures within one ordered phase with analytic free energy and spontaneously broken continuous symmetry are also distinguishable by quasi-local operations. The paper probes this finer structure of state convertibility.
AI.method: Analyze symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of a canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and of a classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in d≥3. Compute the maximum mutual information obtainable by separate measurements in distant regions, extract its logarithmic growth with region radius and the O(1) constant term, and show monotonicity of the constant under quasi-local channels; extend to quantum and multicomponent Villain models.
AI.result: Two distant observers can estimate the shared order direction increasingly well at lower temperature; the maximal mutual information grows as the log of region radius with a leading term uniform across the ordered phase and a constant C(T)=½ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_geom strictly larger at lower T, where Υ(T) is the phase stiffness and c_geom depends only on geometry. Quasi-local channels cannot increase C(T), so it is invariant under two-way conversion, ruling out cooling between distinct temperatures. On finite lattices, vanishing-error cooling requires circuit causal radius growing at least linearly in lattice side length.
AI.conclusion: Temperatures within a single ordered phase are inequivalent resources under two-way quasi-local channels, characterized by a stiffness-dependent invariant C(T); the invariant is also obtained for quantum and multicomponent Villain models, and a stiffness formula is conjectured for general continuous symmetry-breaking patterns.

title: A receiver-side approach to confirm phase randomization in BB84 time-bin QKD with weak coherent pulses
summary: In quantum cryptography using time-bin BB84 protocols, the relative phase of symbol pulses has to be random to avoid vulnerability to coherent attacks. Typically this phase randomization is checked on the sender side. Here, we propose a protocol for monitoring and confirming phase randomization independently on the receiver side during operation. The proposed method can be implemented on the single-photon level without the need for any physical adaptation of the receiver. This can provide an additional tool for monitoring against possible eavesdropping attempts that affect the phase randomization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a receiver-side method to monitor and confirm relative-phase randomization of symbol pulses in time-bin BB84 quantum key distribution, implementable at the single-photon level without modifying the receiver hardware.
AI.motivation: In time-bin BB84, randomized relative phase between symbol pulses is required to resist coherent attacks, but this randomization is conventionally verified only on the sender side, leaving the receiver without an independent operational check.
AI.method: A protocol for monitoring and confirming phase randomization independently on the receiver side during operation, realizable at the single-photon level and requiring no physical adaptation of the receiver.
