AI.result: The approach yields an additional monitoring tool that can detect eavesdropping attempts affecting phase randomization, without receiver hardware changes.
AI.conclusion: Receiver-side, single-photon-level phase-randomization monitoring strengthens time-bin BB84 security assurance by complementing conventional sender-side checks.

title: Ellis: Extremely Fast Quantum Circuit Simulation under Qubit Loss and Leakage
summary: Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: while a qubit remains lost or leaked, every operation acting on it is dropped. Consequently, the Clifford circuit executed differs from shot to shot. This variation breaks Pauli-frame simulation, which constructs each shot by XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single \emph{common reference} measurement record. By rethinking the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation, we show that many key fault-tolerant primitives nevertheless retain a common reference under loss. These include CSS code memory, lattice surgery, and transversal CNOT. Such circuits can therefore be simulated exactly under Pauli noise and loss by a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for the dropped operations. We define \emph{frame-CSS} circuits as those that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model that specifies where qubits can be lost and reloaded. We prove that every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference, and we give a practically near-linear-time procedure that certifies whether a circuit is frame-CSS. We implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package \href{https://github.com/isaachyw/ELLIS}{\textsc{Ellis}} (Efficient Loss and Leakage Invariant-reference Simulation). On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, \ellis{} samples 952{,}000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least $1000\times$ faster than Clifft~\cite{chase2026} and PPVM~\cite{luo2026ppvm}.

AI.tldr: Loss and leakage break Pauli-frame simulation by making the executed Clifford circuit shot-dependent, but the authors show that key fault-tolerant primitives (CSS memory, lattice surgery, transversal CNOT) retain a common reference, formally define frame-CSS circuits, prove they admit a common reference, and provide a near-linear certifier plus a fast simulator (Ellis) achieving ~952k shots/s on the gross code.
AI.motivation: Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: any operation on a lost/leaked qubit is dropped, so the effective Clifford circuit varies from shot to shot. This variation invalidates Pauli-frame simulation, which relies on XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single common reference measurement record. Existing simulators therefore cannot exploit the Pauli-frame speedup under loss/leakage.
AI.method: The authors re-examine the respective roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation. They identify fault-tolerant primitives that preserve a common reference under loss (CSS code memory, lattice surgery, transversal CNOT), and generalize via the class of frame-CSS circuits: circuits that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model specifying where qubits can be lost and reloaded. They prove every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference and give a practically near-linear-time certification procedure. They implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package Ellis.
AI.result: They prove the common-reference property for frame-CSS circuits and demonstrate a near-linear-time certifier. On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, Ellis samples 952,000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least 1000x faster than Clifft and PPVM.
AI.conclusion: Pauli-frame simulation can be extended to loss and leakage for a broad, certifiable class of fault-tolerant circuits (frame-CSS) via per-shot masks for dropped operations, yielding exact simulation under Pauli noise plus loss and order-of-magnitude gains (≥1000x) in sampling throughput over prior simulators.

title: The role of complementarity and quantum correlation in the uncertainty relations and the optimum states
summary: Uncertainty relations are used in quantum mechanics to illustrate the complementarity of two observables, assuming there is a lower bound for the product of their dispersions that depends on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of those observables in an optimum state. In this work, we demonstrate that the complex parameter of the optimum state equation has real and imaginary parts that depend on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation between the observables in the optimum state, respectively. We apply our results to a two-level system, finding that the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of two spin-1/2 projections in the optimum state complement each other and, finally, when the term correlation is used, a lower bound for the uncertainty principle does not depend on any parameter of the optimum state, in contrast to the usual form of the Heisenberg principle.

AI.tldr: A study showing that the complex optimum-state parameter's real and imaginary parts are set by the first-order quantum correlation and the commutator of the two observables, yielding a parameter-free uncertainty lower bound.
AI.motivation: Standard uncertainty relations give a dispersion-product lower bound depending on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutator evaluated in an optimum (minimum-uncertainty) state, but the structure of that optimum-state parameter is not made explicit. The authors aim to decompose this dependence into clear correlation and commutation components.
AI.method: The complex parameter of the optimum-state equation is analytically decomposed, identifying its real part with the first-order quantum correlation and its imaginary part with the commutator of the observables in the optimum state. The framework is then applied to a two-level system, specifically two spin-1/2 projections.
AI.result: The real and imaginary parts of the optimum-state complex parameter are shown to depend on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation, respectively. For two spin-1/2 projections, the correlation and commutator in the optimum state are shown to complement each other, and the resulting uncertainty lower bound becomes independent of any optimum-state parameter.
AI.conclusion: The correlation-based formulation yields a parameter-independent lower bound for the uncertainty principle, in contrast to the usual Heisenberg form, clarifying the distinct roles of quantum correlation and non-commutativity in uncertainty relations.

title: Improving the signal-to-noise ratio through postselection of coincident detections in anticounterfeiting and quantum key distribution
summary: In quantum communications and other photon-counting applications, reliably detecting weak optical signals against a strong noise background remains a fundamental challenge. In this paper, we develop a simple idea: when a signal is carried by pairs (or more generally multiplets) of photons emitted simultaneously, postselection of coincident detections recorded on two detectors makes it possible to improve-sometimes drastically-the Signal to Noise Ratio. Essentially, this is made possible by the fact that genuine and accidental coincidences scale differently with the width of the postselection window. As long as the window remains wide enough to retain detections from the same pair, the genuine coincidence rate is approximately unchanged. In contrast, coincidences formed from independent clicks decrease linearly as the window is narrowed. The resulting signal-to-noise ratio, therefore, increases inversely with the window width. Our approach makes it possible to reveal photon-pair signals that are otherwise hidden beneath a much stronger uncorrelated background. We analyze here applications of this idea to quantum key distribution, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.

AI.tldr: Postselecting coincident detections across two detectors within a narrow time window improves the signal-to-noise ratio when the signal consists of photon pairs/multiplets, because genuine coincidences are window-width independent while accidental ones scale linearly with window width.
AI.motivation: Detecting weak optical signals against strong noise backgrounds is a persistent challenge in quantum communications and photon-counting applications; the paper seeks a simple method to suppress uncorrelated background.
AI.method: Signal photons arrive as pairs (or multiplets) emitted simultaneously; coincident detections on two detectors are postselected within a time window. Genuine coincidences from the same pair are retained as long as the window spans the pair's arrival, keeping their rate roughly constant, whereas accidental coincidences from independent clicks decrease linearly as the window narrows.
AI.result: The signal-to-noise ratio increases inversely with the postselection window width, sometimes drastically, enabling recovery of photon-pair signals otherwise buried under a much stronger uncorrelated background.
AI.conclusion: Coincidence postselection is a simple and effective noise-suppression technique; the authors analyze its application to quantum key distribution, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.

title: Cooperativity-enhanced single-photon emission in a topological quantum emitter chain
summary: Single-photon emitters are one of the key elements in state-of-the art quantum technologies, yet optimizing and manipulating their emission requires precise fabrication of the emitter systems themselves. Here, we propose a route to tailored single-photon emission by exploiting cooperative effects in a topological single-photon emitter chain. Although the involvement of multiple emitters normally suppresses single-photon emission, we show that localized topological edge modes restore single-photon emission and protect against local perturbations. At the same time, cooperative effects occur due to the collective nature of the edge modes, leading to directional emission and linewidth narrowing. Our findings open new possibilities for tailoring single-photon emission by combining cooperativity and topological effects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes tailoring single-photon emission by combining cooperative effects and topological edge modes in a chain of emitters, showing that edge modes restore single-photon emission, protect against local perturbations, and enable directional emission with linewidth narrowing.
AI.motivation: Single-photon emitters are key to quantum technologies, but optimizing and manipulating their emission requires precise fabrication of the emitter systems. A route is needed that relaxes this fabrication burden while still enabling tailored emission properties.
AI.method: The authors exploit cooperative effects in a topological single-photon emitter chain. They analyze how localized topological edge modes emerge in the chain and how the collective nature of these edge modes modifies the emission behavior, including robustness to local perturbations.
AI.result: Although involving multiple emitters normally suppresses single-photon emission, the localized topological edge modes restore single-photon emission and protect it against local perturbations. Meanwhile, cooperative effects from the collective nature of the edge modes produce directional emission and linewidth narrowing.
AI.conclusion: Combining cooperativity with topological effects opens new possibilities for tailoring single-photon emission, offering a design route that is robust to local disorder without requiring precise fabrication of individual emitters.

title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
summary: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,μ$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,μ$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,μ$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

AI.tldr: In a simulated six-qubit spin-chain reservoir, the effect of dephasing and observable choice on learning is strongly task-dependent: coherence mostly helps nonlinear autoregressive prediction, unpredictably affects autonomous limit-cycle generation, and consistently hurts chaotic forecasting.
AI.motivation: The paper asks how dephasing (coherence time T2) and the choice of measured observables shape learning performance in a dissipative quantum reservoir, and whether coherence benefits are universal or task-specific.
AI.method: Six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout; comparisons of single-plus-two-qubit observables versus population-only readout at matched polynomial feature counts, benchmarked against a relaxation-and-dephasing-disabled reference. Tasks: externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals; autonomous generation trained with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation; chaotic forecasting; and a noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor. Evaluated across an ensemble of reservoir realizations.
AI.result: For driven NARMA signals, combined single- and two-qubit observables outperform population-only readout at comparable feature counts, and most tested configurations beat the no-dephasing reference, most strongly at T2 = 1 μs (where total memory capacity drops) and still at T2 = 5–10 μs (where memory is merely redistributed across delays). Autonomous generation shows no clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence. Chaotic forecasting horizons at T2 = 1 μs shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations. On the strange non-chaotic attractor the model yields a smooth, approximately closed orbit, capturing neither the scatter nor the pointwise trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence on learning depends strongly on the task; dephasing is not uniformly detrimental, and observable choice interacts with coherence time to determine performance.

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
summary: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

AI.tldr: CAVQS is a context-aware variational quantum circuit synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution across block boundaries with dynamic pre-measurement reconstruction to reduce two-qubit (CNOT) gate counts.
AI.motivation: Block-based variational synthesis instantiates blocks independently, which limits simplification across block boundaries, and fully unitary synthesis ignores opportunities created by permitted terminal measurements and classical feedforward.
AI.method: CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks (preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local targets to enable cross-block reductions), and for blocks preceding permitted terminal measurements it builds ancilla-free dynamic implementations via a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search plus analytic branch-unitary construction, minimizing expected CNOT cost.
AI.result: On random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% versus QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN on common successful instances; on 4-6-qubit algorithm benchmarks, reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting inter-block context via unitary redistribution and leveraging measurement-enabled dynamic reconstruction yields substantial two-qubit gate savings over independent block synthesis, consistently across random and algorithm targets.

title: A sensitivity-constrained polynomial method for DQC1 query complexity
summary: The polynomial method is one of the fundamental techniques for proving lower bounds on quantum query complexity, particularly in the BQP query model. In this work, we develop an analogue of the polynomial method for the DQC1 query model. We introduce the notion of {\em sensitivity approximate degree} for Boolean functions and show that it provides a lower bound on DQC1 query complexity. We establish several basic structural properties of this new measure. As a first result, we show that every nonconstant total Boolean function on $N$ input variables has sensitivity approximate degree $Ω(N)$, and hence requires $Ω(N)$ queries in the DQC1 model. Thus, unlike in the BQP query model, DQC1 admits no asymptotic query speedup for total Boolean functions. For symmetric partial Boolean functions, we give a complete characterization of the sensitivity approximate degree in terms of the separation between oppositely labeled Hamming weight layers. This yields a tight quadratic separation between sensitivity approximate degree and standard approximate degree, and also leads to tight quadratic separations between DQC1 and BQP query complexities. We further establish quantitative average-case classical simulation theorems for DQC1 algorithms. Finally, we apply our framework to Fourier analysis, obtaining a simple proof of an $Ω(N^{1/4})$ DQC1 query lower bound for the 2-Forrelation problem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the sensitivity approximate degree and a polynomial method for the DQC1 query model, proving that DQC1 admits no asymptotic speedup for total Boolean functions and establishing tight quadratic separations from BQP.
AI.motivation: The polynomial method is a foundational tool for proving lower bounds in the BQP query model, but no analogous framework exists for the DQC1 query model. The authors aim to fill this gap and characterize the query power of DQC1 relative to BQP.
AI.method: They define the sensitivity approximate degree of Boolean functions as an analogue of approximate degree, prove it lower-bounds DQC1 query complexity, and establish its structural properties. For symmetric partial Boolean functions they derive a complete characterization via the separation between oppositely labeled Hamming weight layers, and they develop quantitative average-case classical simulation theorems for DQC1 algorithms, applying the framework to Fourier analysis.
AI.result: Every nonconstant total Boolean function on N variables has sensitivity approximate degree Ω(N), hence Ω(N) DQC1 queries. For symmetric partial functions, the sensitivity approximate degree is fully characterized, yielding a tight quadratic separation between it and standard approximate degree and tight quadratic separations between DQC1 and BQP query complexities. They also obtain an Ω(N^{1/4}) DQC1 lower bound for 2-Forrelation via a simple Fourier-analytic proof.
AI.conclusion: DQC1 admits no asymptotic query speedup for total Boolean functions, in contrast to BQP, while symmetric partial functions can exhibit quadratic gaps; the sensitivity approximate degree provides a tractable and effective lower-bound technique, with average-case classical simulation results and new Forrelation lower bounds.

title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics
summary: Accurate identification of the Hamiltonian governing a quantum system is important for quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable operation of quantum hardware. In practical systems, however, the governing dynamics may vary over time because of parameter drift, changing control conditions, or transitions between operating regimes. In this work, we formulate Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) problem in which a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations and estimates the governing Hamiltonian parameters. We first consider stationary dynamics using a Vanilla-QRL agent and then introduce a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture to track non-stationary dynamics. The framework is evaluated on transverse-field Ising model systems under stationary dynamics, abrupt Hamiltonian switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual Hamiltonian drift. We further compare the proposed approach with a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline and evaluate frozen policies on unseen trajectories. Results show that both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians, while GRU-QRL provides substantially improved tracking under non-stationary dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential of recurrent QRL as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This work frames Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning problem, using a Vanilla-QRL agent for stationary dynamics and a recurrent GRU-QRL agent for non-stationary dynamics, tested on transverse-field Ising models and benchmarked against QGRNN.
AI.motivation: Accurate Hamiltonian identification is essential for quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable hardware operation. In practice the governing dynamics drift over time due to parameter drift, changing control conditions, or regime transitions, yet most identification methods assume stationary dynamics.
AI.method: Hamiltonian identification is cast as a QRL problem where a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations to estimate Hamiltonian parameters. A Vanilla-QRL agent handles stationary dynamics, while a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture is introduced to track non-stationary dynamics. Evaluation uses transverse-field Ising model systems under five scenarios: stationary dynamics, abrupt Hamiltonian switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual drift. A Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline is compared, and frozen policies are tested on unseen trajectories.
AI.result: Both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians. Under non-stationary dynamics, GRU-QRL delivers substantially improved tracking performance compared with the QGRNN baseline.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent QRL shows promise as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems, particularly for tracking non-stationary Hamiltonian dynamics.

title: Efficient calculation of the full Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of entangled biphotons
summary: The spatial biphoton state generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enables applications in high-dimensional quantum information processing and is often described in Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. However, calculating the full LG spectrum for arbitrary radial and orbital angular momentum (OAM) indices requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations. We present a generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral without approximating the phase-matching function. The source geometry can be completely described by a few dimensionless parameters, which reduce to two parameters for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists. Our derived expressions for the full LG spectrum allow for computationally efficient and numerically stable evaluation at high mode orders, addressing a crucial obstacle in previous works. To illustrate our approach, we compare OAM spectra obtained by projection onto the lowest radial order and by radially insensitive detection, and investigate how high-dimensional maximal entanglement can be approached by tuning source parameters. Our results provide a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

AI.tldr: A generating-function method analytically evaluates the full Laguerre-Gaussian spatial spectrum of SPDC biphotons without approximating the phase-matching function, enabling efficient and stable computation at high mode orders using only a few dimensionless source parameters.
AI.motivation: Computing the full LG spectrum of the SPDC biphoton state for arbitrary radial and OAM indices conventionally requires computationally demanding four-dimensional transverse integrations, which is a key obstacle for characterizing high-dimensional spatial entanglement.
AI.method: A generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral while retaining the exact phase-matching function; the source geometry is captured by a few dimensionless parameters (two for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists).
AI.result: Closed-form expressions for the full LG spectrum that are computationally efficient and numerically stable at high mode orders; illustrative comparison of OAM spectra from lowest-radial-order projection versus radially insensitive detection, and analysis of how tuning source parameters approaches high-dimensional maximal entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

title: A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger States Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, Lean examples. Comments welcome
summary: Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating an \(N\)-photon \(D\)-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even \(N\ge4\) when \(D\ge N\). The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum \(\mathcal F\) of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an \((N-1)\times N\) matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes \(ω\) and GHZ target \(Δ\), the row--column imbalance yields \(\mathcal F(ω)=0\) but \(\mathcal F(Δ)\neq0\), contradicting the required equality \(ω=Δ\). Finally, we give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph (and hence no photonic GHZ state generated by probabilistic pair sources conditioned on one photon per detector) exists for any even N ≥ 4 when D ≥ N, using an AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean.
AI.motivation: Photonic GHZ states from probabilistic pair sources admit an edge-coloured, complex-weighted graph representation in which an N-photon D-dimensional GHZ state corresponds to a monochromatic quantum graph; the open question is whether such monochromatic graphs can exist, i.e., whether these sources can produce high-dimensional GHZ states in the relevant parameter regime.
AI.method: A proof discovered via AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean (AlphaProof Nexus). It constructs a weighted sum F of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex; summing over colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an (N−1)×N matrix of effective edge weights. Comparing the graph amplitude ω with the GHZ target Δ, a row–column imbalance gives F(ω)=0 while F(Δ)≠0, contradicting ω=Δ.
AI.result: No complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even N ≥ 4 whenever D ≥ N. The AI-discovered proof is subsequently given a physical interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic pair sources cannot generate N-photon D-dimensional GHZ states with D ≥ N for even N ≥ 4, establishing a fundamental no-go result in this graph-based framework, with the argument certified by machine-checked formal proof and reinterpreted physically.

title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
summary: Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: Non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are shown to be free-fermion-disguised and to admit a Jordan-Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding, with both theorems formalized in Lean; a heuristic line-graph algorithm finds free-fermion fragments of molecular Hamiltonians with performance comparable to non-contextual searches.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian decomposition into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation, and contextual subspace decomposition—expressing Hamiltonians via non-contextual Pauli sets—is one such route. Since contextuality conditions rest on commutation/anticommutation of Paulis, the authors aim to make the connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics explicit.
AI.method: Two central theorems: (1) non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are free-fermion-disguised; (2) such Hamiltonians can be written in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, carrying a Jordan-Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. Both theorems are formalized in the Lean proof assistant. A heuristic algorithm searches for line-graph-based free-fermion fragments and their connected components in molecular Hamiltonians.
AI.result: The space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians is characterized and related to the broader class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. Benchmarked against non-contextual searches on encoded molecular Hamiltonians, the algorithm achieves comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components.
AI.conclusion: The work clarifies which fragments are useful for quantum simulation, linking non-contextuality to free-fermion solvability and providing verified (Lean-formalized) theory plus a practical heuristic for fragment selection.

title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
summary: Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

AI.tldr: Introduces the "code quilt," an ancilla-free construction for directly measuring joint logical Pauli products across multiple codeblocks, analyzed as a subsystem code with distance-preserving conditions and validated empirically on bivariate bicycle and surface codes.
AI.motivation: There is growing demand for fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code, but many existing proposals rely on dedicated ancillary systems. The authors seek a construction that measures multi-codeblock joint logical operators directly, without extra ancillas and using only the qubits already present for idle syndrome extraction.
AI.method: The code quilt is formulated as a subsystem code, with explicit circuits that couple codeblocks to realize the joint logical measurement. The authors give a structural analysis and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the relevant code-capacity distance. Two protocol variants are proposed: (i) direct measurement of the subsystem code's gauge generators—provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but highly practical, increasing physical qubit degree by at most two; and (ii) a variant with more favorable asymptotic properties, though general fault tolerance is not proven. Empirical evaluation spans bivariate bicycle and surface codes, including optimization for sparse, decongested detector bases and circuit-level distance estimates.
AI.result: Code-capacity-distance-preserving quilts were found for 25,000 randomly selected logical operators on bivariate bicycle and surface codes. Sparse, decongested detector bases were optimized, and estimated distance-preserving circuits were identified for a random subset. Decoding experiments show logical error probabilities comparable to idle memory for operations on the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and the distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates of 1.5×10⁻³ to 3×10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: The code quilt provides a practical, ancilla-free route to fault-tolerant multi-codeblock logical Pauli-product measurement, with a simple low-overhead variant and a promising asymptotically better variant. Empirical results on bivariate bicycle and surface codes indicate performance on par with idle memory, supporting its use in modular fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
comment: 15 pages + 7 pages of appendices, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies the "irrealism" of decoding observables as the relative entropy to the closest preparation that leaves the observable undisturbed, and derives exact irrealism frontiers for quantum random access codes (PM and entanglement-assisted) in relation to success probability.
AI.motivation: Quantum advantages in communication tasks are usually attributed to resources like coherence or entanglement, but it is unclear how far decoding observables must depart from having elements of reality to achieve a given advantage. The authors aim to characterize this required irrealism for quantum random access codes (QRACs).
AI.method: An observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; irrealism is defined as the relative entropy to the closest such preparation, capturing local coherence plus correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, they derive the irrealism frontier (least total irrealism per success probability) exactly in every dimension, with an excess-irrealism identity showing Gibbs states of the decoding operator uniquely attain it. They also minimize over decoders, and analyze EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings.
AI.result: Exact irrealism frontiers are obtained in all dimensions for PM codes in mutually unbiased bases; Gibbs states attain the frontier uniquely. For PM codes minimized over decoders, required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not cheapest below success probability 0.833. For EA codes, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the optimal code's contexts, and rank-one projective sender measurements with success probability above 0.815 certify a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.
AI.conclusion: Irrealism provides a unified resource for PM and EA random access codes, yields tight frontiers linking success probability to departure from elements of reality, and enables certification of realism-based nonlocality in shared entangled states.

title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
summary: We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

AI.tldr: Using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits, the paper shows entanglement can propagate to an environment site before a comparably strong local record forms, identifies the leading record as an off-diagonal density-matrix element detectable via Pauli (not population) measurement, and derives optimal state-recovery fidelity from the system plus an environment fragment.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relationship between entanglement spreading, the formation of readable (accessible) records in an environment, and the conditions under which an unknown quantum state can be recovered from the system plus a fragment of the environment, in a setting amenable to exact analysis.
AI.method: An exactly solvable model of a chain of sequentially interacting qubits is analyzed. The authors compare entanglement arrival at later environment sites with local-record strength, decompose the reduced density matrix to isolate the leading off-diagonal record and its measurement signatures, characterize relative-phase accessibility through joint transverse correlations, and compute the optimal recovery fidelity for reconstructing an unknown state from the system and an accessible environment fragment.
AI.result: For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record resides in an off-diagonal reduced-density-matrix element, detectable by a Pauli measurement, whereas a population measurement yields only a higher-order signal. Relative-phase accessibility is captured by joint transverse correlations. Optimal recovery fidelity is derived, and environment-internal interactions are shown to redistribute readable records and alter the region needed for quantum recovery while leaving the system's reduced state unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement propagation, record readability, and quantum recoverability are distinct and not synchronized: records can lag entanglement, are stored off-diagonally, and can be redistributed within the environment without disturbing the system's reduced state, thereby shifting the environment region required for optimal quantum recovery.

title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
summary: Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum circuit that treats measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom, placing two quantum Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in coherent superposition via a "schedule qubit," and shows that schedule interference visibility depends only on the time offset, that one readout outcome reverses the Zeno trend, and that memory-qubit parity measurements distinguish coherent from classical/dephased schedules.
AI.motivation: Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction, in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global state is stationary, the authors seek to explore the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom rather than a classical parameter.
AI.method: Two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit are placed in a coherent superposition controlled by a schedule qubit. The interference visibility between schedules is analyzed as a function of time offset and number of intermediate measurements. A circuit implementation with physical memory qubits is proposed, in which the joint X-basis parity of the memory register is measured to distinguish a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one; gate counts and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit realization are provided.
AI.result: For fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements. For one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, yielding a result complementary to the standard Zeno probability. Measuring the memory register's joint X-basis parity distinguishes coherent from classical or dephased schedules.
AI.conclusion: The Page-Wootters picture motivates the protocol and offers an equivalent stationary representation, but the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation—consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through clock-system correlations.

title: Effect of coupling asymmetry on the spontaneous decay and entanglement of two atoms in a common cavity
summary: We investigate the dynamics and the spontaneous decay of two identical two-level atoms into the vacuum in a cavity at low temperature. We analytically derive the survival probability and the amplitudes of the state of the system by calculating the exact self-energy when the atoms are both initially excited. It is found that moderate asymmetry enhances the decay of the survival probability and increases the entanglement production in either lossless and lossy cavities.

AI.tldr: Two identical excited two-level atoms decaying into a low-temperature cavity vacuum are studied exactly via the self-energy; moderate (not maximal) asymmetry between the atoms accelerates the survival-probability decay and maximizes entanglement generation, in both lossless and lossy cavities.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to clarify how asymmetry between two identical emitters governs their collective spontaneous decay and entanglement dynamics in a cavity at low temperature, a regime where exact treatment of the atom-field interaction is tractable and collective effects are pronounced.
AI.method: The authors analytically compute the exact self-energy of the two-atom system initially in the doubly excited state, then derive the survival probability and the state amplitudes of the full system; the analysis is extended to both lossless and lossy cavities.
AI.result: A moderate degree of asymmetry is found to enhance the decay of the survival probability and to increase the entanglement produced, whereas this behavior holds in both lossless and lossy cavity settings.
AI.conclusion: Moderate asymmetry, rather than perfect symmetry or strong asymmetry, is the optimal condition for faster collective decay and higher entanglement generation in this cavity-QED system, providing a design criterion for controlling two-atom dissipative dynamics.

title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
summary: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.

AI.tldr: An efficient classical randomized algorithm approximates the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions (including attractive Hubbard models) without sign problem, spectral gap, or weak-coupling assumptions.
AI.motivation: Ground-energy estimation for interacting fermions is a central quantum many-body problem. Quantum algorithms give polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families, but classical quantum Monte Carlo suffers from the sign problem and, even with nonnegative expansions, lacks rigorous rapid-mixing guarantees.
AI.method: Reduces ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation, then uses a discretization with controlled energy error to express the quantity as a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli, and applies the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. A sharper arithmetic bound is obtained by controlling the number of independent sampling runs and matrix updates and by using sparse matrices to lower per-update cost.
AI.result: Provides an efficient classical randomized algorithm with rigorous guarantees for the ground energy of conjugate hopping Hamiltonians with conjugate-paired orbital interactions, covering interactions beyond onsite density attraction and requiring no physical spectral gap or weak-coupling assumption.
AI.conclusion: A polynomial-time classical guarantee for ground-energy estimation of structured fermionic systems is achievable, extending beyond prior rapid-mixing and sign-problem-free results while reducing computational cost.

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
summary: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces non-binary detector error models (DEMs) for circuit-level quantum error correction, where each fault location is modeled by a single random variable over its full alphabet rather than being split into independent binary mechanisms, enabling exact representation of any Pauli channel.
AI.motivation: In Stim and most prior work, DEMs are binary: non-binary circuit errors (e.g., a CNOT's 16 two-qubit Pauli errors) are decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. Binary DEMs are only exact for channels that factorize into independent binary parts, and the decomposition inflates the Tanner graph, harming hardware efficiency and decoding performance.
AI.method: The authors define non-binary DEMs in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is a single random variable over its original alphabet (e.g., 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT). They propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging error components that flip the same detectors and observables. They retain belief propagation (BP) with a single scalar message per edge and evaluate surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes, with and without OSD post-processing.
AI.result: Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for factorizing channels. When channels factorize, binary and non-binary DEMs are proven equivalent under degenerate quantum MAP decoding but not under quantum MAP decoding. Numerically, non-binary DEM Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, and BP (with and without OSD) performs better than binary counterparts, with BP+OSD running up to 9.4× faster on a CPU.
AI.conclusion: Non-binary DEMs offer a more faithful, exact description of circuit-level Pauli noise with more compact Tanner graphs, yielding both hardware advantages and improved decoding performance and speed compared to binary DEMs.

title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
summary: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

AI.tldr: Entanglement swapping's ideal functionality is unrealizable against an intermediate node that misreports classical outcomes; a cut-and-choose protocol certifies a bounded misreport rate on untested pairs, with memory as the dominant cost.
AI.motivation: Quantum repeaters rely on entanglement swapping to distribute entanglement over long distances, but the security of swapping in a network where intermediate nodes follow quantum operations honestly yet may lie about the classical outcome has not been characterized. The authors aim to define and achieve a meaningful security guarantee under this misreporting threat model.
AI.method: The paper first analyzes the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping and shows it cannot be realized, since the ideal version gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state while a relabeling node does. It shows honest noise in the ideal setting does not resolve this unless it concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. It then proposes a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the remaining (untested) ones above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, exploiting the indistinguishability of misreporting from readout noise.
AI.result: The protocol yields a quality-of-service guarantee where failure witnesses non-compliance, and untested pairs remain usable (unlike verification schemes that consume certified states), with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate over 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs for minimum noise levels of 0-5%. Memory is the main cost: 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties memory to block size at a weaker rate: a 10^4-qubit memory certifies 14% over 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.
AI.conclusion: Ideal entanglement swapping is unattainable under a misreporting intermediate node, and honest-noise idealization does not fix it. A cut-and-choose protocol provides a practical quality-of-service certification of misreport rate that preserves untested pairs for use, but is limited by quantum memory capacity; block-wise verification trades rate for reduced memory.

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 Extended Data figures, 1 Extended Data table
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: Rapids is a streaming neural decoder co-designed with an FPGA that decodes syndromes in under a microsecond for the distance-19 surface code at 240x lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation needs classical decoders fast enough to match superconducting syndrome generation rates with low latency. Existing speed-optimized decoders sacrifice accuracy, requiring larger codes and more physical qubits to compensate.
AI.method: Co-design of a streaming neural decoder with an FPGA: the network is composed of operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in the device's integer arithmetic. The design extends to color codes and bivariate-bicycle codes, and scales across multiple FPGAs or custom silicon.
AI.result: For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each syndrome round in under a microsecond on a single FPGA with low latency and a logical error rate 240x lower than existing real-time hardware decoders. On the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code it is 16x more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. Distribution over several FPGAs or hardening into custom silicon yields faster, more accurate, or larger-code decoding.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing neural decoders with classical hardware enables fast, accurate real-time decoding, positioning classical hardware as a scalable resource alongside qubits for improving fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
summary: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

AI.tldr: Nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose distinct constraints and must be treated differently: only Markovian noise requires local quantum error correction suppression, while nuisance parameters can be separated from the target signal via optimal coherent control on the full evolution, so Heisenberg scaling remains attainable even when the signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance directions.
AI.motivation: Existing error-correction approaches under Markovian dynamics tend to suppress nuisance responses together with environmental noise. The authors argue this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and overly restrictive, because nuisance parameters and Markovian noise are fundamentally different and thus should not be handled the same way.
AI.method: They build a general framework for quantum sensing where parameters are encoded in a general time-dependent Hamiltonian in the simultaneous presence of nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. Within this framework they derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that achieve it.
AI.result: Heisenberg scaling requires Markovian noise to be suppressed locally via quantum error correction, but does not require nuisance parameters to be eliminated locally—and in general they should not be. Optimally designed coherent control can separate accumulated nuisance effects from the target signal over the entire sensing evolution, so Heisenberg scaling remains attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise.
AI.conclusion: Local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary; distinguishing them from Markovian noise and handling each with the appropriate strategy substantially enlarges the regime where Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general design principle for robust quantum sensors.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
summary: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

AI.tldr: Decoding performance under disordered (spatially/temporally varying) noise is governed by a few information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: entropy sets the threshold and Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold logical failure rate.
AI.motivation: Real devices exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and characterizing this disorder improves decoding, yet theoretical treatments of QEC assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. A theory connecting decoding performance to the statistics of disordered noise channels is missing.
AI.method: Physical error rates are modeled as random variables, so decoding operates with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered channels. The authors derive analytic expressions relating decoding performance to information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution and validate them numerically using maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes under code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise, including distributions from open-access superconducting devices.
AI.result: The threshold is determined by the entropy of the noise distribution, while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Numerics show good agreement with theory across all three noise models and with realistic superconducting-device noise distributions, and the framework yields a quantitative measure of the benefit of noise characterization.
AI.conclusion: Reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of a device's noise distribution can be more informative for realistic error correction than reporting mean or median component error rates.

title: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model
summary: Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.

AI.tldr: Adding a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr term to the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian keeps it lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving the generalized Z4 symmetry, yielding an exact zero-temperature phase diagram with a first-order normal-to-bright transition and an exponentially closing same-sector tunneling gap.
AI.motivation: Collective two-photon light-matter interactions allow pair amplification but destroy spectral confinement, and this spectral collapse prevents a stable thermodynamic bright phase. The paper seeks a Hamiltonian mechanism that stabilizes pair amplification while retaining the symmetry structure of the two-photon Dicke model.
AI.method: Introduce a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction into the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of N emitters. Determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with O(N^-1) finite-size control, obtain the global phase diagram, and validate with symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization up to N = 128.
AI.result: The Kerr term renders the Hamiltonian lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving the generalized Z4 symmetry. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Exact diagonalization through N = 128 supports the predicted density jump and reveals an exponentially closing same-sector normal-bright tunneling gap.
AI.conclusion: Spectral collapse is reinterpreted as the singular zero-Kerr limit of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing two-photon pair amplification.

title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
summary: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

AI.tldr: Simple quantum error-detecting codes (notably a two-qubit repetition code) suffice for sequential entanglement generation over repeater chains under near-term hardware, outperforming unencoded strategies for QKD.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum repeaters are needed for long-distance, trust-free quantum communication. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is attractive for its modest implementation demands and hop-by-hop compatibility with classical infrastructure, but key design choices for such schemes remain unclear.
AI.method: The authors compare design options for sequential entanglement generation with error detection over a repeater chain, using quantum key distribution as the benchmark task. They evaluate simple quantum error-detecting codes (repetition codes, quantum parity codes) against unencoded strategies, and analyze different architectures for generating the initial entanglement.
AI.result: Simple error-detecting codes perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform no-encoding approaches; two-qubit repetition codes may be sufficient in many practical scenarios. Different initial-entanglement architectures are assessed for their relative merits, and moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially offset slower progress in others.
AI.conclusion: Practical repeater schemes may rely on minimal encoding rather than sophisticated codes; modest hardware improvements in select components can compensate, in part, for lagging components.

title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes interleaving quantum position verification (QPV) rounds into a BB84 QKD protocol so that a party's physical position serves as the authentication credential, achieving greater efficiency than prior schemes that ran a full QPV protocol per authenticated bit.
AI.motivation: QKD requires authentication so that honest parties do not unknowingly establish a key with an impersonating adversary. Existing position-based approaches are inefficient because they require running an entire QPV protocol for every bit that needs authentication.
AI.method: The authors design a protocol consisting of a standard BB84 QKD scheme with QPV rounds randomly interleaved, using the position of one party as the authentication credential. They provide an initial security analysis restricted to a specific set of attacks.
AI.result: The interleaved design is reported to be efficient relative to prior approaches, avoiding the per-bit cost of full QPV execution. Security is established only for a restricted attack class.
AI.conclusion: Position-based authentication can be integrated efficiently into BB84 QKD via random QPV interleaving, though the security guarantees remain preliminary and limited to a restricted set of attacks, leaving broader analysis for future work.
