  Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
  Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
  Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise (CHN) problem, show it lies in QMA but is hard for the QCMA hierarchy in the query model, and use it to construct a classical oracle separating QMA from QCMAH while collapsing P, BQP, QCMA, and QCMAH—demonstrating that quantum-proof/state advantages and quantum cryptographic primitives can persist even when classical computation matches all classically-verifiable quantum computation.
AI.motivation: Motivated by Cakan's Codeword-Hash Structure problem (introduced to separate QMA from QCIP), the work seeks to characterize the power of quantum proofs/states over classical proofs. The goal is to determine whether a quantum state or quantum-proof advantage can exist even in a world where classical computers can efficiently solve every problem verifiable with a classical (quantum-verifier) proof, and to show quantum cryptographic primitives can exist without one-way functions or quantum computational advantage.
AI.method: Introduces the Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise (CHN) problem, inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem. Proves that in the query complexity model CHN is in QMA yet hard for the QCMA hierarchy QCMAH = ∪_d QCMA^(QCMA^(···^QCMA)). Constructs classical oracles using CHN to separate QMA from QCMAH under the collapse P^O = BQP^O = QCMA^O = QCMAH^O ⊂ QMA^O, and to build quantum cryptographic primitives relative to such oracles.
AI.result: Establishes a classical oracle O with P^O = BQP^O = QCMA^O = QCMAH^O ⊂ QMA^O and QMA^O ⊄ QCMAH^O. Relative to such an oracle (with P^O = BQP^O = QCMA^O = QCMAH^O), constructs pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives.
AI.conclusion: Quantum state/proof advantages can exist even when classical computers efficiently solve any problem quantumly verifiable with a classical proof. Quantum cryptographic primitives (e.g., PRS with classical keys, copy-protected PKE) can exist even when P = QCMA, so neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage are necessary. This answers an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

title: Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter
summary: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Training a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles—sharing information across a phase diagram then locally fine-tuning—lets quantum samplers reproduce ground-state correlations more accurately than independent fits.
AI.motivation: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter, and selected correlations can guide classical training of a quantum sampler even when full-distribution sampling is hard. The paper asks whether training across related ground-state distributions (rather than fitting each separately) helps the sampler reproduce correlations more accurately.
AI.method: A hypernetwork maps Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram, followed by local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients is derived for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with cost depending on circuit generators. A CDF-KL loss compares selected marginals, and an automated search selects reference calculations near phase transitions. Studied on the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model.
AI.result: On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4×256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits show lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry.
AI.conclusion: Shared training across a phase diagram combined with local fine-tuning is a promising approach for preparing quantum samplers, outperforming independent per-point fitting.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
summary: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes end-to-end quantum algorithms for differential equations (classical-in, classical-out) and delivers a fully implemented algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation with gate cost polylogarithmic in grid size and quasilinear in inverse accuracy, condition-number-independent.
AI.motivation: Prior quantum differential-equation algorithms rely on abstract oracles and assumptions, leaving their practical feasibility and real-world computational advantage unclear. A concrete, fully specified, classically-input/classically-output pipeline is needed to assess genuine quantum advantage.
AI.method: Defines end-to-end quantum algorithms as accepting classical inputs and returning classical outputs, with concrete implementations of the required primitives. For the variable-coefficient LPB PDE, introduces a new grid-based discrete representation enabling efficient operator-oracle implementation, and applies optimal-wavelet preconditioning to obtain a solution cost independent of the discretized operator's condition number. All stages—initial-state preparation, quantum solution generation, and property estimation—are explicitly implemented as quantum circuits.
AI.result: Quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both grid points N_g and inverse accuracy 1/ε; overall gate cost polylogarithmic in N_g and quasilinear in 1/ε; classical preprocessing to construct circuits is also polylogarithmic in N_g and 1/ε; exponential improvement in N_g scaling over classical methods.
AI.conclusion: Provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a practically valuable PDE, demonstrates exponential scaling improvement in grid size over classical methods, and establishes a foundation for assessing practical quantum advantage.

title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
summary: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

AI.tldr: Novel in-place quantum arithmetic algorithms achieve subquadratic gate counts ($O(n^{1+\varepsilon})$) with sublinear (often zero) ancilla qubits for modular multiplication, integer multiplication, and modular inversion.
AI.motivation: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block of quantum algorithms, and their implementation cost significantly affects the viability of many quantum applications. Existing state-of-the-art implementations suffer from high space and gate-count overheads, motivating the search for more efficient in-place arithmetic primitives.
AI.method: The authors present new algorithms for in-place quantum arithmetic. In-place modular multiplication modulo a power of two is performed with a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ gates and no ancilla qubits. Standard in-place integer multiplication with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier uses $O(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ gates, requiring no ancilla for the classical multiplier and logarithmically many ancilla qubits for the quantum case. In-place modular inversion modulo a power of two follows from the modular multiplication algorithm with $O(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ gates and no ancilla. The multiplication algorithms are derived as consequences of a single unified theorem.
AI.result: The proposed algorithms achieve both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts—claimed to be the first such quantum algorithms for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of the fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, requiring only enough space to store the output, which overwrites the input directly.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers highly efficient in-place quantum arithmetic operations with improved space and gate-count overheads compared to the state-of-the-art, unified under a single theorem that may find further application in quantum arithmetic.

title: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators
summary: We propose a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed via numerical estimators that avoids the logarithmic query overhead of amplifying the confidence of estimates before the search. A coherent estimator that is $\varepsilon$-accurate with probability at least $2/3$ on each of $N$ labels suffices to find a $2\varepsilon$-optimal label using $O(\sqrt N)$ base-estimator queries at constant confidence. The query bound and the additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. More generally, suppose a preparation assigns probability mass at least a known $p$ to objective values at most $a$. Without knowing $a$ or the prepared distribution, our algorithm returns a candidate and an estimate $v$ such that, jointly with constant probability, $v$ is $\varepsilon$-accurate for the candidate and $v\le a+\varepsilon$. The algorithm uses $O(p^{-1/2})$ queries to each of the preparation and estimator oracles in the worst case, and the selected candidate can be retained as a quantum state. For preparation width $s_P$ and estimator workspace width $w$, it requires $O(s_P+w+\log\log(4/p))$ qubits, independently of the requested confidence. Applications give worst-case optimal $Θ(\sqrt N/η)$ queries for selecting an $η$-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using $O(ω^{-1})$ preparations and $O((ωη)^{-1})$ elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence, where $ω$ is a lower bound on the guiding state's ground-space amplitude overlap.

AI.tldr: A quantum minimum-finding algorithm that searches over objective values accessed only via noisy numerical estimators, avoiding the log-factor overhead from confidence amplification and achieving worst-case-optimal O(√N) queries.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum minimum-finding amplifies the confidence of estimator outputs before searching, incurring a logarithmic query overhead. The authors aim to eliminate this overhead while handling objectives given by probabilistic ε-accurate estimators.
AI.method: A coherent estimator (ε-accurate with probability ≥2/3 per label) is used directly inside a variational-style search that operates on objective values, tolerating additive error rather than requiring high-confidence estimates. Generalized to a preparation that places known probability mass p on values ≤ a, the algorithm outputs a candidate plus estimate v, using O(p^{-1/2}) queries to preparation and estimator oracles, retaining the candidate as a quantum state, and requiring O(s_P+w+log log(4/p)) qubits independent of confidence.
AI.result: Finds a 2ε-optimal label with O(√N) base-estimator queries at constant confidence; query bound and additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. Yields worst-case optimal Θ(√N/η) queries for selecting an η-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation with O(ω^{-1}) preparations and O((ωη)^{-1}) controlled-evolution queries.
AI.conclusion: Quantum minimum-finding can operate directly on imperfect estimators without logarithmic confidence-amplification overhead, giving optimal query complexity, low qubit cost independent of confidence, and improved applications to expectation selection and guided ground-energy estimation.

title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
summary: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.

AI.tldr: Above a constant temperature threshold, local noncommuting qudit Gibbs states show exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI) for arbitrary tripartitions, establishing a uniform Markov property; this is proven via a classical representation using projective 2-designs that admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights.
AI.motivation: Conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge because of noncommutativity, which obstructs proofs of information-theoretic decay bounds for noncommuting Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Construct a classical (quasiprobability) representation of the Gibbs state in an overcomplete basis; although such representations generally carry negative weights, a decomposition based on projective 2-designs yields a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperature, circumventing the noncommutativity obstruction.
AI.result: Exponential decay of CMI is proven for any spatial tripartition A ⊔ B ⊔ C not necessarily covering the whole system (uniform Markov property), together with exponential decay of mutual information. Separability of high-temperature Gibbs states follows as a byproduct.
AI.conclusion: High-temperature Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians are uniformly Markov and separable, and in the framework of mixed-state phases of matter they lie in the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.
